1:1: The second year of Darius the king implicitly means the second year of the reign of Darius as king.
The sixth month of the Hebrew calendar includes August and September on Western calendars.
Here one part of the prophet Haggai, his hand, represents all of him in bringing the word of the Lord to the returned exiles.
The term word represents a message that the Lord conveyed by using words.
1:2: The phrase The Lord of Armies is a title for God that indicates his great power. It describes him as the commander of heavenly armies.
The phrase This people refers to the people of Judah who had returned from exile in Babylon.

As the introduction to Haggai discusses, here and often throughout the book of Haggai, the word house means “temple.” The people are speaking of the temple as if it would be a house in which God lived, since God’s presence would be there.
1:4: The Lord is using the question form for emphasis.
1:5: Here, the heart figuratively represents the thoughts.
The Lord is speaking of how the returned exiles have been living as if that were a series of ways or paths that they were walking along.
1:6: In this culture, as in many cultures today, the water was not safe to drink, so people drank wine made from grapes. This wine contained a low level of alcohol. The Lord is emphasizing that the people do not have enough to drink to satisfy their thirst. If they did, they would also experience a slight stimulating sensation. The Lord is not suggesting that drunkenness is a good thing.
The Lord is speaking as if the returned exiles were literally putting their wages in a punctured bag. The image suggests that when they have expenses, they do not have money available to meet them.
1:9: The Lord is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say.
The Lord is speaking as if he had literally blown on the crops that the Judeans brought home. The image is of the wind blowing hard and carrying off grain.
The Lord is using the question form for emphasis.

The Lord is speaking as if the Judeans were literally running back to their homes whenever they had the opportunity to return to them. He means that they are eager to improve their own homes, even though they do not care about the temple.
1:10: כָּלְאוּ שָמַיִם מִטָּל וְהָאָרֶץ כָּלְאָה יְבוּלָהּ
The Lord is speaking as if the heavens and the earth were living things that could actively withhold dew and produce from the Judeans.

The Lord is speaking as if dew fell from the heavens, that is, from the sky. He means implicitly that not only has rain not been falling from the sky, dew has not even been forming on the ground overnight.
1:11: In this verse, the Lord uses a series of repetitive phrases to show that the effects of the desolation he has called for are comprehensive. A series of phrases like this is called a litany. “And I have called for desolation upon the land and upon the mountains and upon the grain and upon the new wine …”
Here, grain, new wine, and oil represent wheat and barley, grapes, and olives, of which they are the products.
The Lord is using one part of the Judeans, their hands, to mean all of them in the act of working.
1:12: וַיִּשְׁמַע … בְּקוֹל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיהֶם וְעַל־דִּבְרֵי חַגַּי הַנָּבִיא
Here the term voice represents what the Lord said by using his voice and the term words represents what Haggai said by using words.
בְּקוֹל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיהֶם וְעַל־דִּבְרֵי חַגַּי הַנָּבִיא
Here a single idea is expressed through two phrases connected with and. The second phrase tells by what means the action of the first phrase was accomplished.
Here one part of the Lord, his face, represents all of him.
1:14: Here one part of Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people, their spirit in each case, represents all of them.
Here Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people are described as if they had literally been asleep and the Lord woke them up.
1:15: The sixth month of the Hebrew calendar includes August and September on Western calendars.
2:1: The twenty-first day of the seventh month on the Hebrew calendar is near the middle of October on Western calendars.
2:3: The Lord is using the question form for emphasis.
The pronoun that refers to the former glory of the temple.
The Lord is using the term eyes by association to mean sight. Sight, in turn, represents attention, perspective, and judgment.
2:4: The Lord is using this expression to refer to the Judeans who have returned from exile. The phrase means the same thing as the term “remnant” in 1:12 and 1:14. However, the phrase “the people of the land” often has a different meaning elsewhere in the Bible. In other passages, it refers to the Canaanites who were living in the region before the Israelites arrived.
2:5: The Lord is using the term word to mean what he said to the Israelites by using words when he made a covenant with them.

By The word that I covenanted with you, the Lord is referring to what he has just said, “I am with you.” the Lord made this promise to the Israelites when they came out of Egypt. See, for example, Exodus 29:45–46, “And I will live among the sons of Israel and will be their God.
With this statement, the Lord is asserting that he is indeed fulfilling his covenant promise to be with the Israelites.
2:6: עוֹד אַחַת מְעַט הִיא וַאֲנִי מַרְעִישׁ

These phrases Yet once and it will be a little while may mean similar things. The first phrase may mean “after only one more period of time.” The second phrase says basically the same thing but adds the information that this will be a brief period of time. The Lord may be using the two phrases together for emphasis.

The Lord is speaking as if he would literally be shaking all of creation. The image is that of a great earthquake. (People in this culture considered the sky to be a solid object above the earth, so the Lord could shake that as well as the earth with a great quake.) It becomes clear in the next verse that the Lord is actually using all of creation to represent “all nations” in their relationship to his chosen people.

The Lord is using the two main components of creation, the heavens (the sky) and the earth, to mean all of creation. He is then using the two main components of creation below the sky, the sea and the dry land, to mean the entire world in which humans live.
2:7: The Lord is speaking as if he were literally going to shake the nations with an earthquake. It is clear from the context that this represents the Lord changing the attitude of the nations.
2:8: The implication of this statement seems to be that the Lord can promise that the nations will bring their treasure to the rebuilt temple because all of that treasure actually belongs to him.
2:9: Here, as in many other instances throughout the book, the Lord is speaking of his temple as if it were a house in which he lived.

By this place, the Lord most likely means Judea and especially Jerusalem. The enemies of the Judeans destroyed the previous temple, but the Lord is promising here that he will now cause the nations to be at peace with them so that enemy armies do not destroy the rebuilt temple.
2:10: The twenty-fourth day of the ninth month on the Hebrew calendar is near the middle of December on Western calendars.
2:12: The Lord is using a hypothetical situation in order to teach.
The expression holy flesh refers implicitly to meat that has been offered to the Lord as a sacrifice. Only priests could eat such meat.

The priests mean implicitly that while touching holy flesh makes a person holy (and therefore conveys certain privileges but also makes the person subject to certain restrictions, see Leviticus 6:27), that person does not communicate this holy state to objects that he touches.
2:13: Haggai implicitly means a person who has died, and he is speaking specifically of that dead person’s body.

Haggai and the priests share the knowledge that if an Israelite touches a dead body, something that is ritually unclean, then that Israelite becomes ritually unclean himself for a certain period of time (see Numbers 19:13). Such a person is not allowed to take part in public worship.
This is the counterpart to the priests’ answer in the previous verse.
2:14: The word Thus refers implicitly to a state of uncleanness.
In this context, the terms people and nation both refer to the Judeans who have returned from exile. The Lord is using the two terms together for emphasis.

Here the Lord is using the term face to mean his presence, by association with the way people can see the face of someone who is present. Presence, in turn, represents the Lord’s judgment by association with the way that he would assess anything that came to his attention in front of him.
The Lord means implicitly that the Judeans are unclean because they have not obeyed him and rebuilt his temple.
The Lord is using one part of the Judeans, their hands, to mean all of them in the act of working. The reference is specifically to their work of growing crops and raising animals.
By there, Haggai implicitly means an altar that the returned exiles had set up at the temple site. This is described in Ezra 3:1–6.
2:15: The word before refers back in time to the whole period after the Judeans returned from exile.
The Lord is using one part of the building process to represent the entire process of rebuilding the temple.
2:16: By twenty, the Lord most likely means twenty ephahs. An ephah was equivalent to about 22 liters.

The expression from the press probably describes a certain quantity of wine, a “press-measure,” the amount that a winepress would produce from a single pressing of a full load of grapes. However, it is no longer clear exactly what this quantity was.
2:17: The Lord is using this expression to mean that the Judeans did not obey him and rebuild the temple. Instead, they continued to disobey, as if they had nothing to do with the Lord.
2:18: As in 2:15, the word before refers back in time to the whole period after the Judeans returned from exile. The twenty-fourth day of the ninth month means that date in the second year of Darius, as 2:10 indicates.
2:19: The Lord is using the question form for emphasis.
2:21: The Lord is using the two main components of creation, the heavens (that is, the sky) and the earth, to represent all of creation.
2:22: The Lord is referring to the ruling authority of kingdoms by association with the royal throne on which the rulers of those kingdoms sit.
וְהָפַכְתִּי מֶרְכָּבָה וְרֹכְבֶיהָ וְיָרְדוּ סוּסִים וְרֹכְבֵיהֶם
The Lord is using two components of an army, its chariot teams (the chariots and their riders) and its cavalry troops (the horses and their riders), to mean the entire army.
The Lord is not referring to a specific chariot and rider. He means all of the chariots and riders in the armies of the kingdoms opposed to the Judeans.
Here the word fall means “die” by association with the way someone who dies will fall to the ground.
Here, the sword represents a violent death.
The Lord is speaking of a fellow soldier as if he were literally the brother of another soldier whom he killed.
2:23: The Lord is using the term day to refer to a specific time.

A signet ring was a special ring that a ruler could use to imprint an official seal on a document. This ring bore the ruler’s name or some symbol representing him. The ruler would roll up an important document and put wax on it, then press the ring into the wax to create an official seal. If the document had this mark on its seal, people would know that what was written in the document was written with the king’s authority and had to be obeyed.

The point of this comparison is that Zerubbabel would be an instrument of the Lord’s authority, just as a ruler uses a signet ring as an instrument of his authority. All the nations would have to obey Zerubbabel’s commands because Zerubbabel would be commanding them with authority that the Lord had entrusted to him.
